doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: The health of jazz and prodigy young players
summary: She says players are healthier, balancing inner and outer knowledge, and cites young prodigies.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Being in this hotel right now crawling with jazz musicians and educators and everything, it kind of skews this question perhaps, but how do you feel about the health of jazz these days and for the future?
Well people are healthier while they play it.

Less things that are — you know, but we know more about the body too, so that’s kind of nice. The energy is better. And a lot of people learn so fast in the schooling, these kids learn so fast. It would be nice if we could, well you know, try to balance the inner knowledge, I think that’s the thing that has to happen now because we’re kind of going for the outer knowledge and at some point it’s just like the NASDAQ dropping way down. I think we have to get that together with the inner knowledge so that the human knowledge gets associated fully with the musical knowledge. But it’s taking place. It’s very interesting. Well when I went to hear Chick he had just gotten an e-mail from an eight year old boy, I didn’t hear the end of the story, Chick was going up to Boston to play, but this little boy, or he was seven years old, he had transcribed like Chick’s solos and he could play them, and then he could do free improvisation. So he sent an e-mail with some of his free improvising. And Chick said it sounded very mature, really great. So they were going to meet in Boston. That’s where the little boy lived. So it’s like they were ten and twelve, well the Monk competition was won by a ten year old in third place.

Yeah Latin percussion. Ten years old. That was this year. And then Maria Schneider was telling me, we did some big band, we split a big band concert, and she was telling me about this horn player from Sicily that was like ten or eleven years old, just kind of leading this whole band and having incredible knowledge of how to make the rhythm section, which was not together, sound like it was together. And I’m like okay it was teenagers, now they’re going down into the single digits. Like the wind chill this winter.
Yeah, wow. You wonder if they’re not possessing someone’s spirit from—
